items.title: Hearthwork's premise, as a list
items.where: Hearthwork: Taking Turns, P1
items.your_version:
Hearthwork: Taking Turns Lending & Borrowing Adulthood

Hearthwork is what I call my peer-counseling framework, which combines various other frameworks I'm familiar with. The basic premise is, peers take turns of equal length to privately listen to each other with respect and warm, positive regard. They don't try to interpret what's really going on, give advice, or fix the other person's life in the session. 

This is a "middle path" kind of relationship, that threads itself between ordinary friendship (so you're not "clienting" to your friends) and professional therapy (which gets saved for the more severe issues). Modern life rarely gives us anything like this, and your little one might really need it.

It also helps us with the borrowed adulthood practice. When you take turns listening with a good peer, on an equal footing, their warmth and the way they hold space for you are ideal for borrowing the Nurterer role and what that feels like. The Protector role can also be borrowed from the way they keeping what you say private, and the way you both stop when the turn's time is up.  

But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do." It's hard sometimes, but they agree to keep that to themselves during the session. Instead of telling you what to do, they might ask the right question at the right moment so you can hear your own Guide. There's also no pressure to answer. Then you trade places, and it's your turn to keep "Here's what you should do" to yourself.

items.title: The three jobs a peer can lend you
items.where: Hearthwork: Taking Turns, P2
items.my_version: Some of what the three grown-up jobs do can come from outside you, too. When you take turns listening with a good peer, as equals, their warmth and the way they stay with you lend you the Nurturer for a while. Keeping what you say private, and stopping when the time's up, lends you the Protector. If you say no, they don't push. But they don't act as your Guide, or decide what your experience means. Maybe they're thinking, "Oh, I know what this is about," or "Here's what you should do." They keep it to themselves. A question from them at the right moment can help you hear your own Guide, and what you answer is up to you. Then you trade places, and it's your turn to keep "Here's what you should do" to yourself.

items.title: Borrowed adulthood, and whether it's therapy
items.where: Hearthwork: Taking Turns, P3
items.my_version: The peer doesn't become your permanent parent, though. They show you a capacity, help you get the hang of it, and give it back to you, which is borrowed adulthood in its healthiest form (a driving instructor isn't planning to drive you around forever either). Is that therapy? Well, not the mainstream kind, but yes, for sure. Professional therapy's still useful for what it does, and peers and community do something else, so a serious healing path can include both.

items.title: Show Up When Nothing's Wrong (5 words)
items.where: Show Up When Nothing's Wrong, P2
items.your_version: Watch how your love sounds to your little boo, in context. "I care about you" can be patient, or it can be "I care about you, now hurry up and feel better." Getting close can be too much, too, the way kids squirm away from an aunt they barely know who goes in for the big hug, and then climb all over the uncle who's just sitting there. Knowing that love is in you somewhere counts for a lot, and you're borrowing something you already know how to do.

items.title: When the Spiritual Relationship Hurts (48 words)
items.where: When the Spiritual Relationship Hurts, P2
items.your_version:
Being the grown-up doesn't mean controlling everything yourself, though. After a betrayal like that, part of you might want to. We can use Niebuhr's Serenity Prayer here to help: "God, grant me the serenity
to accept the things I cannot change
the courage to change the things I can
and the wisdom to know the difference." (Replace "God" with universe if you wish.)
items.my_version: Being the grown-up doesn't mean controlling everything yourself, though. After a betrayal like that, part of you might want to. Spiritual support can help you act where it's yours to act, and let go of outcomes and other people's choices where it isn't. The Serenity Prayer is exactly to remember that.

items.title: Make a Simple Vow (3 words)
items.where: Make a Simple Vow, P2
items.my_version: "I know you're in there. I love you. You don't have to love me back or trust me yet. I can't promise that nothing painful will happen. Or that I'll always know what to do, or never react badly. But I can promise to tell you the truth and listen when you're angry. I'll make our life together safer where I can, and take the next step I can see to protect you. When I fail, I'll come back to make it right. You don't have to believe these words. Watch what I do."

items.title: Untangling the Belonging Bargains (11 words)
items.where: Untangling the Belonging Bargains, P1
items.your_version: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from what I call the "belonging bargains" which pull you away from your own inner-knowing in return for belonging. Your friends probably have unwritten rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that's kind to you might have expectations that look at face value like just being a good member.  It can help to write down the unspoken rules your family ran on, like "Boys don't cry." Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent for a sibling, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

items.title: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone (1 word)
items.where: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone, P2
items.my_version: That's exactly why I was crying for 14 years. Beginning at the age of 12, when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people, I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren't, was selfish. I had this poster in my room that really resonated with me, by the famous socialist, Eugene V. Debs. I told this to a therapist in college and she actually agreed it was a good reason to be depressed!

items.title: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone (13 words)
items.where: When Being Happy Feels Like Abandoning Someone, P4
items.your_version:
What I found, once I started cultivating my own happiness, was that I got a lot better at helping other people toward theirs. So do your part for people who are suffering (which might sometimes just be modeling how to live, i.e. doing nothing different), and skip the part where you have to be miserable too.

Some friends or family really might not like it when you get happier, though. Some of them might pull away, while others might try to keep dragging you back into the old misery, since misery loves company. On the other hand, I wouldn't automatically classify everyone as envious just because they don't feel comfortable with you anymore, as it could be something you've done while unaware.

items.title: Dating While You Heal (52 words)
items.where: Dating While You Heal, P1
items.your_version:
Maybe you'd rather that your support came from a lover, as well. Lots of people open a dating app in the middle of the night, hoping someone will make it all stop hurting. 🙈 We call that "co-dependency" (although the term is not literally negative, it has become to carry this connotation). If that's you hitting the Swipe button right now, my suggestion is to let the dating game wait. Let your friends and the steady people around you do their part to support you as you learn to support yourself more. 

That doesn't mean you have to be completely healed before you date, but romance should follow when two people really love each other and want to build a life together. It won't rescue you from the pain of your life, nor reward you for healing, and it sucks to mess up a beautiful relationship because of unhealed trauma. Believe me, I've been through it. I wrote a whole romance guide, mostly due to this.

items.title: If You Really Did Hurt Them (7 words)
items.where: If You Really Did Hurt Them, P2
items.your_version: Are you really sorry for what you did, or are you just trying to feel sorry because they're upset? If you've said what you really feel, without dressing it up or justifying it, then let that be that. There's no guarantee they'll understand it, and they might need to mull it over for a while before they're even willing to hear what you said. That's how anger works, it grips you. Meanwhile, guilt may keep shouting at you. That doesn't tell you the whole conflict was your fault, nor does it prove they're manipulating you.
